seo.title: AI Audio Research | Igor Szuniewicz
seo.description: Bachelor Thesis: Can AI generate sound effects in real-time for video games?

header.title: Can AI Generate Game Audio in Real-Time?
header.description: For my bachelor thesis, I tried to figure out if AI can generate sound effects fast enough for games. I built a Unity prototype that talks to AI models through a Python server. Spoiler: It's not ready yet, but I found a workaround.

setup.title: What I Tested and Why
setup.intro: Games ship with hundreds of pre-recorded sound files. Every gunshot, footstep, explosion — all WAV files someone recorded in a studio. AI could generate these on the fly instead. Each sound would be unique, adapting to what's happening, no gigabytes of audio files. The catch: latency. If a sound arrives even 100ms late, players notice.
setup.approach: I built a prototype. Unity sends requests to a Python server, which calls an AI model and streams back the audio. I tested three models: ElevenLabs (cloud API, best quality but the latency jumps around), MMAudio (video-to-audio model I adapted for games, runs locally), and AudioGen (Meta's text-to-audio, most consistent but still slow).

results.title: Measured Latency
results.subtitle: Generation times for each model, compared to what games actually need. Log scale — the differences are that large.

tooltip.elevenlabs: Cloud API. Best quality, but latency varies wildly — 1s to 12s on the same day.
tooltip.mmaudio: Video-to-audio model adapted for game use. Runs locally, 2-5s per sound.
tooltip.audiogen: Meta's text-to-audio. Most consistent at ~3s, but still too slow for real-time.
tooltip.cached: Pre-generated sounds served from memory. 21-55ms delivery time.

elevenlabs.note: Cloud-based, quality depends on server load

mmaudio.note: Local, originally designed for video soundtracks

audiogen.note: Most consistent, but 3s is still 3s too slow

solution.title: Caching Sounds Ahead of Time
solution.story: None of the models came close to real-time. The fastest was still over a second — about 60x too slow for a gunshot. I had added a simple cache early on just to avoid generating the same sound twice. Then I saw the cache hit times in the logs: 21-55ms. That's fast enough.
solution.insight: The question changed from "how do I make AI faster" to "when do I call AI?" Generate sounds during loading screens or quiet moments. Store them in a cache. Serve them instantly when the player needs them. When a sound gets used, generate a new one in the background to replace it.

loading.label: Loading Screen
loading.description: AI generates sounds in the background while the player waits

play.label: Player Acts
play.description: Sound plays from cache in under 55ms

refill.label: Background Refill
refill.description: The system generates replacement sounds for next time

solution.usecases: This works best for predictable sounds — ambient audio, cutscene effects, gunshots with limited fire rates. It breaks down with very frequent events like footsteps, where the cache empties faster than AI can refill it.

closing.conclusion: AI audio isn't ready to replace traditional game sound design. It's too slow for real-time use. But if you cache sounds ahead of time, it can add variety and cut down on file sizes for certain use cases.
closing.reflection: The most interesting part wasn't any specific model. It was realizing the problem isn't about making AI faster — it's about calling it at the right time. The tech will keep improving, but even now, when you generate matters more than how fast you generate.

session2.title: Session #2 Findings: The Local AI Reality (Failed)
session2.content: Date: 2025-12-05. We attempted to run MusicGen and AudioLDM2 locally on student hardware (No CUDA). Result: 4-10 seconds latency per sound. Conclusion: Pure local AI is currently unfeasible for twitch-reaction gameplay. We need a faster solution.

session4.title: Session #4 Findings: Stress Testing the Hybrid Model
session4.content:
Date: 2025-12-05. We stressed the new 'Hybrid' architecture (Procedural + Cloud AI). 
- Burst Test: 100 simultaneous requests handled in <200ms.
- Throughput: 2253 generations/sec achieved.
- Latency: 5.02ms (Procedural) vs 2-4s (Cloud).
The hybrid approach is confirmed viable for production.
